baseline.note: The validator pins this count. A capability may only leave capabilities[] by appearing in retired[] with a reason, because deleting an island used to make the registry validate CLEANER rather than louder.
baseline.note_unused_fact_types: MEASURED 2026-10-02, and it corrects a natural misreading. A query for declared fact types produced by no capability returns four: apk, pcap, token, evidence_source. The first three look like dead declarations, and it is tempting to conclude the three matching capabilities (mobile.apk.static, net.pcap.analyse, crypto.jose.parse) do not declare what they produce. They DO -- all three declare their facts, and all three now carry an invoke. The types are unused because the capabilities declaring them have never RUN IN A MISSION, not because their output is unspecified. evidence_source is a different thing entirely: it is a capability attribute used to count independent instruments, not an artifact any capability emits, so it must never be counted here.
baseline.note_q5_unreachable:
MEASURED END TO END 2026-10-02, and it is a shape problem rather than a missing tool. Q5.vuln-shape has no reachable instrument. Its only target-scoped candidate, fuzz.differential.parse, declares two seed inputs whose producers are crypto.jose.parse and forensics.memory.artefact -- and both producers are observed and correctly wired. Verified on the real binaries rather than by reading: crypto.jose.parse invokes crypto-lab/tools/analyze.mjs --file {target} --json, and pointed at a PE it refuses with 'not a compact JWS: expected 3 dot-separated segments, got 2' and EXITS 3, which its own success_when already documents as bad input. Pointed at a real compact JWS it exits 0. forensics.memory.artefact invokes forensics-lab/tools/analyze.mjs --target {target}.

So neither producer is broken. They refuse correctly when handed the wrong KIND of thing, and that is the whole problem: mission.ps1 has one -Target, and this axis needs three different kinds of subject -- a JOSE token, a forensic memory image, and a lab target. Q5 is not dark because a tool is missing. It is dark because the mission can name exactly one artefact and Q5 needs three heterogeneous ones.

Two refutations are kept because both looked right first. First: 'these labs build their own fixtures, so no extra parameter is needed' is true of the LOOPS -- crypto-lab/tools/loop.mjs reads only --json and generates its own tokens, and forensics-lab/tools/loop.mjs:38 hardcodes const TARGET = path.join(WORK, 'target') -- but the invoke blocks point at the inner ANALYSERS, which do take an external subject. The loop and the instrument are different things and a mission calls the instrument. Second: 'fuzz.differential.parse wants two artefacts, so it needs a peer selector' is also true and also not the blocker, because its two missing inputs are not two paths; they are a token and a structure produced upstream.

What would light the axis is now stated precisely: a mission able to name MORE THAN ONE artefact with HETEROGENEOUS types. A second path would not help -- native.function.match is the only capability that wants two of the same thing and it is not on this axis. Naming the shape exactly is what separates this from the speculative -Artefact parameter considered and correctly rejected earlier, when the premise had not been measured.

The misattribution risk was checked and does not exist: a PE substituted into the JOSE analyser exits 3, so a mission records a loud failure rather than crediting the lab's own token to the mission's target.
baseline.note_q5_three_reasons:
Q5.vuln-shape is dark for THREE INDEPENDENT REASONS, and the third is the one that matters. (1) Its only target-scoped candidate, fuzz.differential.parse, declares its subject a lab_target. (2) Its two seed producers are lab analysers whose subjects are lab-built scenario directories, verified by measurement rather than by reading. (3) THAT CANDIDATE DECLARES ITSELF NOT COVERABLE BY A GRANT -- gate.requires_verdict is false, and gate.Get-GrantableIds grants only where it is true. Measured: crypto.jose.parse hit exactly this wall, refused as skipped_not_in_grant with a correct invoke and a correctly seeded fact.

Reason (3) is not an engineering problem and must not be solved as one. Flipping the flag would be weakening a safety marker to improve a metric, which is the error this project has refused all session. It is recorded as an OWNER DECISION on the three capabilities carrying it -- crypto.jose.parse, re.corpus.solve and fuzz.differential.parse -- and none of them had a reason recorded until now, which is itself the defect R22 closes: a capability can declare itself unrunnable by a grant without saying why.

evidence_families._definition: Which FAMILY of instrument produced a fact. Independence is a property of the INSTRUMENT, not of the tool id and not of this label: two capabilities that drive the same instrument are ONE opinion however they are labelled, and two different decompilers are also one opinion (fact_types.evidence_source says exactly this). The enumerated values below are the permitted set; R18 fails the run on anything else, and R18 also fails when two capabilities sharing one instrument declare different families. Correcting a label here cannot change what the mission gate believes about independence -- the gate must derive the family axis from the instrument -- but a registry that disagrees with itself is a registry nobody can reason about.
evidence_families.decompiler: reconstructs executable code into a higher-level language: Hex-Rays IDA and Ghidra both land here, and two of them agreeing is ONE opinion held twice, not corroboration
evidence_families.static-analysis: NOT a separate family. Retained only so the value is not silently re-used; no capability should carry it, because on this estate it existed solely to relabel one idalib-mcp capability and thereby manufacture a second family
evidence_families.dynamic-observation: watches a running subject: a live page over CDP, a live process
evidence_families.dynamic-instrumentation: injects into or attaches to a live process to observe or alter it
evidence_families.structural-parser: decodes a self-describing container without executing it: JOSE/JWT, zip, png
evidence_families.capture-analysis: reads recorded traffic rather than live traffic
evidence_families.artefact-parser: reads host artefacts left on disk: prefetch, SRUM, registry hives
evidence_families.package-inspection: reads a packaged artefact as built: APK manifest, DEX, resources
evidence_families.binary-similarity: matches functions across two binaries by scoring, without proving equivalence
evidence_families.differential-oracle: compares two implementations of the same parser and treats a disagreement as the finding
evidence_families.practice: solving self-built exercises; proves technique, not transfer
evidence_families.disassembler: reconstructs a machine instruction stream WITHOUT lifting it to a high-level language: capstone and similar code-generation libraries. Distinct from 'decompiler' because it performs no lifting, no type recovery and no control-flow reconstruction -- it is the only family here that states an OPERAND WIDTH, which is measured, not assumed: see native.disasm.capstone's negative control and the pairing study. Added 2026-10-02 after measuring that capstone independently identified the exact addresses Ghidra left as unresolved DAT_ references AND carried the byte-vs-dword width that Ghidra's output omitted. THIS IS NOT THE static-analysis RELABEL ESCAPE: that escape re-declared ONE instrument under a second name, which R18 also blocks by instrument identity. capstone is a genuinely different library with no decompiler in its lineage. What it does NOT buy is confirmation of MEANING -- it corroborates structure and operands, not what the code does.
evidence_families.certificate-verifier: A certificate-verifier decides whether a byte range is a valid encoding of a CERTIFICATE. It is not structural-parser: that family parses a PE IMAGE structure, while this decides whether the bytes inside the SECURITY directory are DER at all, using a different implementation (OpenSSL) from the one that located them (pefile). And it is not trust: no member of this family checks that a chain roots anywhere or that a digest matches a file. der_parsed:true means well-formed ASN.1, which is a far weaker statement than signed.
evidence_families.packet-reader: A packet-reader parses the capture FILE FORMAT itself -- global header, per-packet headers, then enough of the link and network layers to count. It is not capture-analysis, which means shelling out to a dissector, and not structural-parser, which means reading an executable image. Two readers agreeing on a capture is agreement between two implementations of the format, which is the only kind of agreement that is worth calling corroboration.

_comment: Capability contracts, so an orchestrator can compose labs it can introspect. This is NOT an inventory -- manifests/tools.json records what is installed. A capability here states what it consumes, the typed facts it produces, what it requires, what it proves, what it does NOT prove, and a negative control that must fail. 'state: observed' means the probe below was actually run; the summary is what it printed. Verify with: python scripts/registry-verify.py. isolation_check.polarity: SUCCESS IS EXIT 0. Do not compare this to a negative control; it asserts that the station is uncontaminated, and its failure is an emergency rather than a finding.
isolation_check.note:
ISOLATION INVARIANT, NOT A NEGATIVE CONTROL, AND IT WAS FILED AS ONE. trustcheck.mjs answers a different question from every other control in this registry: not 'what would make this capability wrong' but 'has the station been contaminated'. It asserts that zero lab certificates reached the machine and user root stores and that the Windows system proxy is unconfigured. It exits 0 when the isolation HELD, which is the opposite polarity from a control, and the registry recorded expect_exit=1 against it -- meaning the one moment this project most needs to hear from it, a silent success would have been recorded as a failure.

It was ALSO attached to two capabilities at once (web.js.cdp and net.pcap.analyse), so even on its own terms it could not localise which one was implicated. That is R19's argument applied to a control, and R19 never had a control-side half.

Measured: exit 0, printing 'PASS WinHTTP proxy is not configured  Direct access (no proxy server).', 'PASS no certificate landed since the baseline run  unchanged since <ts> (machine 15, user 0)' and 'ISOLATION HELD: zero lab certificates in the machine/user root stores, no system proxy.'

negative_control.plan_reason: OPEN GAP, NOT AN OBSTACLE: no negative control has been written for this capability. The registry previously carried trustcheck.mjs here, which asserts MACHINE ISOLATION (no lab certificate installed, no system proxy) and exits 0 when the isolation held. That is not a negative control -- its polarity is inverted -- and attaching one isolation check to two capabilities also meant it could not localise which was implicated. It now lives in isolation_check, where it is still run. What remains here is the honest admission: this capability can produce evidence and has nothing yet that could refute it.

This entry does not authorise running a third-party or untrusted sample on this station: that is the isolated_vm lane, or a stop. dynamic.device.frida is NOT superseded by this entry and was not edited; that entry is the Android device lane of the same instrument and is correctly absent.
capabilities.composition_note: WHY THERE IS NO `invoke` BLOCK, measured rather than assumed. An invoke is what makes a capability CALLABLE, so its absence is real and a planner is right to mark this entry not-runnable rather than route it as if it were. I tried to write one and the validator refused all three honest shapes, against a copy of this registry with the block spliced in: (A) an argv carrying the instrumentation itself (`Interceptor.attach(t,{onEnter:function(){...}})`) fails R16 -- the braces of a JavaScript object literal are read as a `{placeholder}`, so it reports `placeholder {console.log('HIT');} in invoke.argv has no substitution source`; (B) an argv carrying spaced JavaScript fails R10 as `an invoke argument looks like a joined command line`; (C) the clean shape, `-l <file>.js`, fails R10 with `invoke names 'mobile-lab/frida/hook.js', which does not exist in this repo` -- and writing that hook script is not in this entry's write scope. So the edge `native.ida.list_functions --(native.func.addr)--> dynamic.win.frida` is declared and true but currently SOFT: nothing binds the fact into a command line because there is no command line. The one-line fix is an owner action outside this file: add a hook script under mobile-lab/, then declare `runner: frida` with argv `['<venv>\Scripts\frida.exe','-f','{target}','-q','-t','6','-l','mobile-lab/frida/hook.js']` and `consumes_fact: native.func.addr`. Until then the loop cannot execute this composition, and saying so here is cheaper than letting a plan imply otherwise.

inputs.name: target
inputs.note: a Windows PE this repository built, copied out of the repo before it runs. The probe uses a %TEMP% copy, never the repo binary in place.

inputs.name: function
inputs.note: the IMAGE-space address the static analyser reports, consumed as the RVA SOURCE and nothing more. It cannot be handed to Interceptor.attach as it stands: fact_types.address says 'an address in the target's own address space', and a static VA is an address in the IMAGE's address space. This capability rebases it against runtime.module.base. The negative control is what makes that distinction measured rather than pedantic.

facts.note: the image base of the attached process as the process actually mapped it, read from Process.mainModule.base. This note originally read 'four different bases for one binary ... per-process and per-run, never reusable', and that was OVERSTATED: re-measured 2026-10-02, five consecutive runs of the same binary under the same name all returned 0x7ff666bb0000, while an earlier run the same day returned 0x7ff79e010000. So the honest statement is that it is stable within a session and differs between them, against PE ImageBase 0x140000000 with DllCharacteristics 0x8160 (DYNAMICBASE=True). The rule that follows is unchanged and still load-bearing -- read it at runtime, never hardcode it -- but the reason is that nothing about it is guaranteed, not that it demonstrably moves every single run. Overstating a measurement to make a rule sound stronger is the error this registry exists to prevent, in either direction.

a module export resolved to its live address inside the target. Measured: Module.getGlobalExportByName('printf') = 0x7ffcf0e5d280 in the injected process. This is the one address source that works without any static analysis, because an export name is in the loaded image.

an RVA plus runtime.module.base, summed: the value handed to Interceptor.attach. Measured: 0x1080 + 0x7ff7c3a30000 = 0x7ff7c3a31080, accepted by Interceptor.attach with no error. This fact says the address is ATTACHABLE; it does not say a callback fired, and does_not_prove says so explicitly.

invalidates_on: the process exits or is re-spawned: the image base is re-randomised every run, so a runtime.* address is valid for exactly one process lifetime

requires.install_note: Frida is NOT on PATH and is NOT in the system Python. It lives only in the objection virtualenv at Mobile-Android\objection\.venv\Scripts\. A probe written as bare `frida ...` is a probe that fails on this station, which is why both tool probes spell the full path.

reach.containment_note: The honest class, and chosen for the measurement rather than for the validator. This capability spawns a process on THIS station and injects into it, so the blast radius is this host: one named, self-built PE, under the station's named-process rule. isolated_vm would be false here -- there is no VM on the path of anything measured in this entry -- and picking it to make a check pass is the exact failure mode this registry is under repair for. The class that WOULD be right for a third-party sample is isolated_vm, and running one here is a stop, not a containment choice.
reach.note: exec_target is true because the capability RUNS the binary, which is why containment is pinned at all. fs_write is false for the registered probe: it reads the PE and the process image and writes nothing to disk. That is a statement about the probe command below, not a general promise about every Frida script.

proves: that Frida 17.17.0 is installed on this station and can spawn-gate and inject into a self-built Windows PE: `Spawned ... Resuming main thread!`, `Process terminated`, exit 0, against c01-stringobf.exe sha256 2d59a3c5d3281782e254ed84d14f43768251096240cb85c492f56018b56fbf09

the runtime image base of the attached process, and that it is NOT the PE ImageBase: 0x7ff7c3a30000 measured against ImageBase 0x140000000, and it moved between every run of the same binary in one session (0x7ff6732f0000, 0x7ff6d22d0000, 0x7ff642d00000, 0x7ff7c3a30000)
that a module export resolves to a live address inside the target: printf = 0x7ffcf0e5d280

that a SYMBOL NAME DOES NOT RESOLVE on this class of target: DebugSymbol.fromName('main') returned 0 on a statically linked MSVC binary, while the export name resolved fine in the same script and the same run

that module_base + RVA lands on real, attachable code: base+0x1080 = 0x7ff7c3a31080, and Interceptor.attach accepted it with no error (the first 16 bytes there were read in a companion run, not in the probe: 48 89 54 24 10 89 4c 24 08 48 81 ec 98 00 00 00, the /Od prologue of a function taking (rcx,rdx))
that the SAME RVA handed over unrebased does not quietly misbehave, it faults -- see the negative control
does_not_prove: THAT ANY INTERCEPTION HAPPENED. The probe attaches an Interceptor and no onEnter callback fired, and this entry does not claim it did. Measured reason: on Windows the `frida -f` CLI resumes the main thread BEFORE the injected script is loaded -- the target's own `usage:` line appears ahead of the first line of the script, and a companion hook on ExitProcess did not fire either. Interception WAS measured separately, through the Python API ordering spawn -> attach -> create_script -> load -> resume, where onEnter did fire and wrote a witness file naming the same address. That ordering is NOT the command registered here, so it is recorded and not claimed: the probe proves the instrument reached the process and resolved addresses, not that it caught a call.

that this reaches past this station. It is host-process instrumentation of Windows-local PEs and nothing else. It covers no part of the Android device lane, and dynamic.device.frida remains the (absent) entry that says so.

that a symbol name can be used to find code. DebugSymbol.fromName('main') returned 0, so a hook address on this class of target must be an RVA plus the runtime module base -- never a symbol name, and never the static VA.
anything whatsoever about a third-party or untrusted binary. Every measurement here is against a binary this repository authored; this entry does not widen that, and does not authorise it.

that the device lane works. `frida-ps -ai` HANGS on this station for 300 s and never returns, because there is no device. A hang is not a refusal, so it is deliberately neither the probe nor the negative control.
anything about what the target's code MEANS. This entry proves the instrument reached a process, resolved exports, and refused a wrong address. Reading the logic is what the static entries are for.
gate_must_not_delegate: frida -f on any binary this repository did not author
frida -U, frida-remote, frida-ps -ai: any remote or device session
frida -p <pid> / -n <name>: attaching to a process this station did not spawn
Interceptor.replace, Memory.patchCode: altering the target's code or memory rather than observing it
capabilities.gate_must_not_delegate_why: Measured, not read. (1) This host ASLRs the image (DllCharacteristics 0x8160, DYNAMICBASE=True), so an address handed over without rebasing does not silently hook the wrong thing -- it faults, which is exactly what the negative control shows and exactly why the rebasing rule is a boundary rather than a style preference. (2) `frida-ps -ai` on a device-less host does not fail, it HANGS for 300 s and never returns, so a lane that is supposed to refuse must never be entered through that command: a hang is not a refusal. (3) The target side is a red line, not a policy knob -- an untrusted sample run on this host is a STOP, and the measured reach here is exactly one named, self-built process under station_under_named_process_rule. (4) The CLI's own resume-before-load ordering is an instrument defect, and it is the dangerous kind: it makes a probe look like a working hook when no callback fired. That is the instrument being wrong, not the subject, and no verdict may lean on this entry until the ordering is under the analyst's control.

probe.prepare_note: The probe needs a target. It is the estate's own self-built crackme, copied to %TEMP% and never run from the repo directory. Run `prepare` first, or the probe fails for a reason that has nothing to do with Frida. The JavaScript uses backtick template literals on purpose: it is passed inside PowerShell single quotes, and embedded double quotes are stripped by the native argument builder, which turns this probe into a SyntaxError on the first attempt (measured).

Resuming main thread! | usage: ... <password> | FRIDA_WIN module_base=0x7ff7c3a30000 | FRIDA_WIN symbol_main=0 | FRIDA_WIN export_printf=0x7ffcf0e5d280 | FRIDA_WIN rebased_main=0x7ff7c3a31080 | Process terminated | PROBE EXIT=0 | NOTE: no `FRIDA_WIN HIT main` line was printed -- no callback fired, and does_not_prove says so.

evidence_binding.reason: Honest state, not a gap papered over. The probe WAS run on this station by the agent that added this entry, from a clean %TEMP%\fridaprobe each time, and the console output above is copied verbatim from a run of the command now sitting in this file rather than summarised from another session's transcript. What is NOT retained: no stdout log file, no hash of the run itself, nothing on disk that re-derives the numbers -- only the sha256 of the TARGET binary (2d59a3c5...), which pins what was probed and not what the probe printed. negative_control.command: & 'D:\Software\Tool\WorkStation\debugger\Mobile-Android\objection\.venv\Scripts\frida.exe' -f "$env:TEMP\fridaprobe\target.exe" -q -t 6 -e 'var m=Process.mainModule;console.log(`NEG_CTL module_base=${m.base}`);console.log(`NEG_CTL handing the STATIC va 0x140001080 straight to Interceptor.attach`);Interceptor.attach(ptr(`0x140001080`),{onEnter:function(){}});'
negative_control.expect_output_note: expect_exit is the contract; this line is corroboration. It is written to frida's ERROR stream, so capture it with 2>&1 -- run unpiped, the line can be interleaved away while the exit code stays 1. Measured stable over four consecutive runs: exit 1 every time, line present every time when stderr was captured.
negative_control.why: It must fail, and it must fail for its OWN reason. Measured, same binary, same run, seconds after the probe: `Error: access violation accessing 0x140001080`, exit 1. The reason is the address SPACE, not a typo: 0x140001080 is the genuine image-space address of main (PE ImageBase 0x140000000 + rva 0x1080, rva 0x1080 lying inside .text whose VA is 0x1000 with virtual size 0x156d0, and IDA recovering main there with size 0x17e), so it is unmapped only because DYNAMICBASE moved the image to 0x7ff7c3a30000. The probe, one command earlier, attached cleanly at base+0x1080. Two other obvious controls were rejected rather than shipped: an obviously bogus address such as 0xDEADBEEF would fault too, but it cannot tell 'you failed to rebase' from 'any bad address faults', so it would pass for an unrelated reason; and `frida-ps -ai` does not fail at all, it hangs, so it is not a control.

Second, its machine-readable output is not stdout: the run summary is printed as human text and the structured record is written to fuzz-lab/out/last-run.json (:289), so there is no stdout field for fact_map to bind (mission.ps1:355-361). capabilities.root_reason: Genuine root: it is handed a binary path and runs Ghidra headlessly on it. The Ghidra install and the analyzeHeadless wrapper are REQUIREMENTS, not capabilities, so there is nothing upstream to declare an edge to. It is a producer (native.ghidra.summary, native.ghidra.c) that no declared capability consumes yet.

The verifier sampled 8 of 20 and still found three -- which is the argument for making R20 mechanical rather than re-auditing by hand.

unbound.reason: UNBOUND, AND THE PREVIOUS 'BOUND' WAS FALSE. R20 forced this entry to admit it. The artifact used to look bound because invoke.fact_map sent outdir to 'native.ghidra.c' -- but this entry never declared that fact key, so the binding pointed at nothing. This entry drives the Python API in the order spawn -> attach -> create_script -> load -> resume, and it DOES intercept. One instrument, two orderings, two claims -- and the difference is measured, not argued.
capabilities.composition_note: WHY A SIBLING RATHER THAN AN EDIT. Editing dynamic.win.frida to claim interception would make the entry describe something its registered probe does not do. So the CLI entry keeps its narrower, true does_not_prove and this entry carries the wider, also-true claim. native-lab/tools/frida_spawn_gate.py holds the recipe and is committed, because a recipe that lives only in %TEMP% is not a capability, it is a rumour.

capabilities.composition_note: WHY IT EXISTS, in one measurement. On crackme-corpus/out/c01-stringobf.exe main at RVA 0x1080: IDA Pro inlined the XOR key constants as 18/11/90 and 26/5/51; Ghidra left two of them as DAT_140017344 and DAT_140017342 with NO width, which is dangerous because read as the natural u32, DAT_140017342 is 734042; capstone, containing no decompiler whatsoever, emits `movzx r9d, byte ptr [rip+0x16259]` -> 0x140017342 byte=90 and `mov r8d, dword ptr [rip+0x16254]` -> 0x140017344 dword=11. Same values IDA propagated, plus the WIDTH, because the movzx prefix says byte and the bare mov says dword. **So it is not merely a second opinion on structure: it is the only one of the three instruments that states the fact whose absence made Ghidra's output a trap rather than merely incomplete.**

Registering this family must not be read as having resolved the acceptance question, and the mission's unresolved verdict stands until someone runs the chain and reads whether the RESULT is defensible, not merely whether the gate turned green.

Passing an image-space address, or using an RVA as a raw file offset, yields zero instructions or garbage; the first draft of this script did exactly that and the wrapper now refuses rather than reporting an empty success.

capabilities.title: Report whether a Windows PE carries an Authenticode certificate table, and decode its WIN_CERTIFICATE header -- without verifying anything
capabilities.scope_note: READ-ONLY on the target. Reads IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_SECURITY from the PE optional header and, if present, the WIN_CERTIFICATE header it points at. It never executes a target and never contacts a network: no revocation checking, no chain building, no OCSP, no CRL.
capabilities.composition_note: WHY IT IS THE CHEAPEST REAL EXPANSION OF THE THINNEST AXIS. Coverage measured 2026-10-02 across the seven question types showed Q6 -- 'what token/signature/key handling is this' -- resting on ONE instrument, crypto.jose.parse, which is JOSE/JWT only. For a Windows PE the signature handling lives in the same optional header native.pe.packer and native.pe.container already read, so this costs no new dependency, no install and no disk. The trap it encodes is the one that makes this non-obvious: IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_SECURITY's VirtualAddress is a FILE OFFSET, not an RVA, unlike every other data directory. Mapping it through the section table produces a plausible address in the wrong place.

proves: THAT A CERTIFICATE TABLE IS PRESENT OR ABSENT, on a self-authored fixture and on a real binary. Measured: the fixture returns signed:true with security_offset 143872, dwLength 48, wRevision 0x200, wCertificateType 0x2, and its blob reading back the authored ASCII marker; every corpus binary returns signed:false with an empty directory. Two inputs, opposite answers, from the same code -- which is the only thing that makes 'unsigned' mean anything.

does_not_prove: THAT THE BINARY IS TRUSTED, OR THAT ITS SIGNATURE IS VALID. NOTHING IS VERIFIED. No chain is built, no certificate is parsed, no hash is recomputed over the image, no revocation is checked, no timestamp is examined. `signed: true` means exactly 'there is a WIN_CERTIFICATE here'. A binary whose image was modified after signing still reads signed:true here, and the self-authored fixture reads signed:true with no key and no signature at all. Any trust decision needs a tool that actually verifies, and this is not one.
THAT AN ABSENCE MEANS UNSIGNED BY CHOICE. A repacked or tampered binary can have its certificate table stripped, which reads identically to one that was never signed. Absence is not provenance.
THAT THE PKCS#7 BLOB IS WELL FORMED. It is located and hashed, not parsed. The blob_sha256_prefix is an identity, not a validation.
ANYTHING ABOUT A THIRD-PARTY BINARY. Corpus targets only.

(4) The fixture generator APPENDS to the file and REWRITES the directory entry, so pointed at a real signed binary it produces something that claims to be signed by nothing, which is the most dangerous artefact this tool can make.

capabilities.title: Match known behavioural rule patterns in a self-built Windows PE with capa 8.x, headless
capabilities.scope_note: SELF-BUILT CORPUS TARGETS ONLY. It reads the binary and matches rules; it never executes it, never touches the network, and writes only to stdout.
capabilities.composition_note:
REGISTERED BECAUSE AN AUDIT FOUND IT MISSING ENTIRELY. capa is installed and works headlessly, and searching the registry for the string 'capa' returned all 23 entries -- because the word appears inside 'capabilit*y*'. It had no entry at all. What makes it worth registering is the property this registry has been short of: it is TARGET-SCOPED. It takes a path, so a mission can actually route it, unlike the five capabilities whose subject is a token, a pcap, an APK, a loopback URL or a lab artefact.

AND IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT Q5.vuln-shape, which is the axis currently dark. Wiring it there would have lit Q5 up on paper while answering a different question. Measured on c01-stringobf.exe, its 14 hits are 'change memory protection', 'PEB access', 'create or open file' -- those are BEHAVIOURS present in the code, not trust boundaries. Putting a rule matcher on the 'where does it trust something it should not' axis is precisely the relabel escape R18 exists to prevent, and the entry would have been false the moment it was written.

inputs.note: a Windows PE. Measured: crackme-corpus/out/c01-stringobf.exe.

THAT THE BINARY IS TRUSTWORTHY WHEN NO RULE MATCHES. Absence of a match is absence of a known pattern, not evidence of safety -- the same shape as 'not packed' meaning no signature matched.

THAT THE 14 RULES ARE ALARMING. They are what a CRT-linked Windows binary normally matches. The count is only meaningful against a per-binary baseline, and none exists yet.

reporting a rule hit as observed behaviour rather than as a pattern present in the code

(2) The count has no denominator: 14 hits on a plain CRT binary is unremarkable, and quoting it as a number without a baseline is the confident-wrong-number failure this project keeps finding. (3) A rule match is a static pattern; the gap between 'the code can do this' and 'it did this' is exactly what dynamic.win.frida.intercept exists to close.

capabilities.title: Independently parse a PE certificate table's bytes with OpenSSL ASN.1 and say whether they are DER
capabilities.scope_note: SELF-BUILT CORPUS AND FIXTURE TARGETS ONLY. It reads the file and shells out to openssl asn1parse on an extracted temporary .der, which is deleted in a finally block. No network, no execution of the target.
capabilities.composition_note:
ADDED BECAUSE INDEPENDENCE, NOT BECAUSE COVERAGE. Q6.crypto measured 1 of 2 callable capabilities working, and its single working instrument was native.pe.authenticode carrying family structural-parser -- one instrument, one family, so the independence gate could never pass there. This is a SECOND FAMILY answering a different question, not a second label on the first.

AND IT FOUND A REAL DISAGREEMENT, which is the strongest evidence in the registry for keeping it. native.pe.authenticode's own does_not_prove says it verifies nothing. Pointed at this repository's own signed fixture it reports dwLength=48, wRevision=0x200, revision_is_2_0=true -- a plausible, cheerful header. MEASURED, the 40-byte body is the ASCII string ARSENAL-FIXTURE-NOT-A-REAL-SIGNATURE and `openssl asn1parse -inform DER` rejects it outright: 'error:0680009B:asn1 encoding routines:ASN1_get_object:too long', exit 1.

Neither instrument is wrong. pefile is right about the header; OpenSSL is right about the DER. Only together do they say the thing that matters: the arsenal's own 'signed' fixture is not a signature, and an instrument reading only the header would never have noticed. That is what a second opinion is FOR, and it is not visible from either side alone.

inputs.name: binary
inputs.note: a Windows PE. The SECURITY directory stores a FILE OFFSET, not an RVA; this tool resolves it the same way native.pe.authenticode does and says so in its source rather than quietly agreeing with it.

facts.note: dwLength, wRevision, wCertificateType, revision_is_2_0, is_pkcs_signed_data, body_bytes. Measured on the fixture: dwLength 48, wRevision 0x200, wCertificateType 0x2, 40 body bytes.

TRI-STATE, and the three states are not interchangeable. true = OpenSSL parsed the bytes as DER. false = OpenSSL rejected them and reason says why. null = there is no SECURITY directory, so there is nothing to verify. 'nothing to verify' and 'what is there is not valid' are different findings and MUST NOT share a value -- collapsing them is how an unsigned binary gets reported as a broken signature. Measured: null on c01-stringobf.exe, false on the fixture, with reason 'ASN1_get_object:too long'.

requires.install_note: Both already present. Measured OpenSSL 3.5.7. No download, no build, no PATH change. Runs in well under a second against a fixture -- the cheapest capability in the arsenal, which is worth knowing because it makes this the natural second instrument to run whenever a first one reports something surprising.

reach.proc_spawn_note: Declared because it invokes openssl.exe as a child. fs_write is also true and honestly so: it writes a temporary .der under the system temp directory and deletes it in a finally block, which is WHY write_scope is temp_dir and why escalation_class is owner_word rather than none.

proves: THAT A SECOND INSTRUMENT CAN DISAGREE WITH THE FIRST AND BE RIGHT, measured on this repository's own artefact. native.pe.authenticode reads dwLength=48 / wRevision=0x200 / revision_is_2_0=true off the fixture and is not wrong; OpenSSL rejects the same 40 bytes with ASN1_get_object:too long and is not wrong either. The fixture's certificate is the ASCII string ARSENAL-FIXTURE-NOT-A-REAL-SIGNATURE.

THAT Q6.crypto HAS A SECOND FAMILY. Q6 measured 1 of 2 working, one instrument, one family, which is the state the independence gate exists to refuse. This entry carries certificate-verifier, a genuinely different question from reading the table.
does_not_prove:
THAT THESE TWO INSTRUMENTS ARE FULLY INDEPENDENT, AND THE MISSION'S OWN OUTPUT SAYS SO. Verified in a Q6 mission on 2026-10-02: independence PASSES with '2 capabilities across 2 instruments (openssl+pefile, pefile) carrying 2 distinct families'. Read that instrument list rather than the verdict: the two SHARE pefile. This entry uses pefile only to LOCATE the SECURITY directory; the DECISION is OpenSSL's DER decoder, which is a genuinely separate implementation and is where the disagreement with native.pe.authenticode actually comes from.

The shared part is not decorative. If pefile misread the DATA_DIRECTORY entry, both instruments would be wrong together and the second opinion would be worthless -- the independence gate counts instruments, and two instruments that share a locator are only as independent as that locator. It is recorded here rather than left to be discovered later, because a partial overlap that is written down is a limitation and the same overlap written down as '2 independent instruments' is a false claim.

THAT ANYTHING IS TRUSTED, SIGNED OR SAFE. ASN.1 PARSING IS NOT TRUST. der_parsed:true means the bytes are well-formed ASN.1 -- nothing here checks that the chain roots anywhere, that the digest matches the file, or that the signer is who it claims.

THAT A REAL SIGNATURE WAS REJECTED. What was rejected is a fixture whose payload SAYS it is not one. Rejecting it proves the instrument can tell DER from non-DER; it says nothing about a genuine signature, because this repository has no genuine signed binary to point it at.
ANYTHING ABOUT TRUST BOUNDARIES. Not a Q5 instrument and not offered as one.

THAT pefile IS WRONG. It is not. It reads a header and reports it accurately; this tool checks the layer below. Two instruments each being right is the whole mechanism, and collapsing either into 'the other one is broken' destroys it.

gate.escalation_reason:
CORRECTED BY R6 AND R8, WHICH CAUGHT AN UNDER-DECLARATION. This entry was first written with escalation_class 'temp_write', a class that does not exist, and no write_scope at all -- so it looked identical to a capability that writes only into the case directory. It does not: it writes a .der into the system temp directory and deletes it in a finally block.

The rule's own comment is the reason this is owner_word and not none: 'writing anywhere else is not a runtime self-decision', and only case_dir write may be class none. Small and bounded is still outside the boundary, and the honest way to say so is the strict reading rather than the comfortable one. No instrument in the arsenal should choose to write outside its case directory without an Owner word, and if this one is ever run under a mission that is the grant that governs it.

Counting both as structural-parser would make Q6 report two instruments when it has one implementation and one reader, which is precisely the relabel escape R18 exists to stop.

capabilities.title: Parse a pcap with no library and no tshark: counts packets, flows, ports and DNS direction
capabilities.scope_note: READS ONE FILE. No network, no execution, no writes, no temp files. It parses the 24-byte global header, the 16-byte per-packet headers, and then Ethernet / VLAN / IPv4 / IPv6 / TCP / UDP far enough to count.
capabilities.composition_note:
ADDED FOR INDEPENDENCE, AND THE INDEPENDENCE IS REAL THIS TIME. net.pcap.analyse answers capture questions by shelling out to TShark 4.6.8, and it was the arsenal's ONLY capture-analysis instrument, so Q4.data measured one instrument in one family and the independence gate could never pass there. A second front-end over the same C library would have been one implementation held twice; this is a from-scratch reader in pure Python with no third-party dependency at all, so agreement between the two is corroboration rather than a restatement.

MEASURED 2026-10-02, all five lab captures, both instruments, packets AND DNS direction:
  dns-basic.pcap 4/4 dns 2/2 vs 2/2 | dns-txt.pcap 4/4 dns 2/2 vs 2/2 |
  http-basic.pcap 10/10 dns 0/0 vs 0/0 | odd-port.pcap 26/26 dns 0/0 vs 0/0 |
  tls-clienthello.pcap 14/14 dns 0/0 vs 0/0 -- ALL AGREE.

AND THE FIRST COMPARISON ATTEMPT WAS WRONG, WHICH IS WORTH RECORDING. It reported a disagreement: tshark '0/0' against the reader's 2/2. The cause was the comparison script, not either instrument -- tshark's dns.flags.response prints the STRINGS 'False' and 'True', and the script compared them to '0' and '1', so it counted nothing and reported a phantom discrepancy. tshark in fact sees all four DNS rows and agrees exactly.

That is the 'an error is not a zero' trap in a new costume, and it nearly became a recorded finding about a working tool. A disagreement between instruments is the most interesting thing this pair could produce, which is precisely why a buggy comparator is dangerous here: it manufactures the interesting result.

inputs.name: capture
inputs.note: a classic libpcap file. The corpus is GENERATED, not committed: net-reverse/lab/gen-pcaps.mjs writes five synthetic captures to %TEMP%\net-reverse-lab\pcaps (override NET_REVERSE_PCAP_DIR).

facts.note: packets, bytes_on_wire, captured_bytes, frames_over_snaplen, ipv4, ipv6, tcp, udp, other_proto, distinct_flows, top_ports. Measured across the corpus: dns-basic 4 packets, http-basic 10, odd-port 26, tls-clienthello 14, dns-txt 4.

dns_queries and dns_responses counted from bit 15 of the DNS flags word. Measured: 2 queries and 2 responses on each of dns-basic and dns-txt, 0 and 0 on the other three. A COUNT TAKEN FROM A HEURISTIC, not from dissection: this reader matches on port 53 and reads two bytes. TShark dissects and agrees here, which is what makes the number worth having -- on a capture with a non-standard port or a malformed DNS header, only the dissector would be right.

requires.install_note: NO THIRD-PARTY DEPENDENCY. struct and ipaddress are in the standard library, which is the whole point: scapy and dpkt are not installed on this station, and a second reader built on either would have had to be installed first. Runs in well under a second, which makes it the cheapest cross-check in the arsenal.

reach.proc_spawn_note:
CORRECTED BY R8, WHICH WAS RIGHT AND I WAS WRONG. This first read proc_spawn:false on the reasoning that nothing is shelled out to. That reasoning conflated two things: running `python pcap_reader.py` IS a child process, and R8's floor says exactly that -- any capability with a probe.command or an invoke.runner spawns something, precisely so that deleting the declaration makes it falsifiable.

What actually distinguishes this entry is narrower and is the claim worth making: it spawns ONLY its own interpreter and no analysis tool. net.pcap.analyse spawns TShark; this spawns python and reads the bytes itself. That is why the two are independent rather than one implementation behind two front-ends.

proves: THAT Q4.data HAS A SECOND, GENUINELY INDEPENDENT IMPLEMENTATION. Measured on all five lab captures: packet counts agree with TShark 4.6.8 (4/4, 4/4, 10/10, 26/26, 14/14) and DNS query/response counts agree too (2/2, 2/2, and 0/0 on the three with no DNS). Two implementations written against the same file format in two languages is what corroboration means.
THAT A CAPTURE CAN BE READ WITHOUT ANY ANALYSIS TOOL. No tshark, no scapy, no dpkt, no subprocess. If TShark disappeared this capability would still answer.
does_not_prove: ANYTHING ABOUT CONTENT. There is no reassembly and no TLS decode. A DNS name split across packets is not read, and an encrypted payload is not decoded. Agreement with TShark is corroboration of the COUNTS only, and neither instrument here says anything about what any packet contained.

THAT pcap.dns_direction IS A DISSECTION. It is a port-53 match plus one bit. On a capture using a non-standard DNS port, or carrying a malformed DNS header, this reader would be wrong and TShark would be right. The two agree on THIS corpus, which is a fact about the corpus and not a general property.

THAT THE CORPUS IS REPRESENTATIVE. All five captures are SYNTHETIC and generated by net-reverse/lab/gen-pcaps.mjs. Two readers agreeing on five generated files is evidence about the format and about those files; it is not evidence about real traffic.

THAT THE FIRST COMPARISON SHOWED A DISAGREEMENT. It did not. That was a bug in the comparison script and is recorded in composition_note so the phantom discrepancy is not rediscovered and mistaken for a finding.
